captions.monthly_revenue.png: Monthly net revenue from December 2010 to December 2011. Values are in GBP thousands. The series shows a strong seasonal build-up to November–December, with December 2011 partial (only 1–9 December observed).
captions.monthly_orders.png: Monthly count of distinct invoices. Order volume follows the same seasonal shape as revenue, confirming that the seasonal peak is demand-driven rather than price-driven.
captions.top_products.png: Top 10 physical products by net revenue. Revenue is concentrated in a small set of decorative and giftware lines; product-level revenue is far more concentrated than unit demand.
captions.top_products_qty.png: Top 10 products by unit volume. The volume leaders differ from the revenue leaders: cheap, high-turnover items sell in bulk but contribute less value per unit.
captions.country_analysis.png: Revenue by country (top 15). The United Kingdom dominates, followed by a small group of EU markets; the long tail of countries each contributes a very small share.
captions.quantity_distribution.png: Distribution of quantity per invoice line, clipped at 100 units for readability (maximum observed = 80,995). The distribution is right-skewed with a median of 4 units; most lines are small retail quantities.
captions.unitprice_distribution.png: Distribution of unit price, clipped at £100 for readability (maximum observed = £13,541.33). The median price is £2.08, indicating a low-value, high-volume product mix with a thin high-price tail.
captions.revenue_distribution.png: Distribution of invoice values clipped at the 99th percentile. Most invoices are small; the mean is pulled upward by a small number of very large wholesale orders.
captions.quantity_outliers.png: Box plot of order quantity on a log scale. The box spans the interquartile range; the many fliers above the upper whisker are genuine large purchases, not automatic errors.
captions.customer_spending_box.png: Distribution of total spend per customer on a log scale. The wide spread confirms a high-value minority coexisting with a large base of low-spend customers.
captions.customer_segmentation.png: Customer counts by RFM segment. The majority of customers fall into low-frequency, low-value segments, while Champions are a small but commercially critical group.
captions.correlation_heatmap.png: Spearman correlation matrix for invoice-level variables. Invoice value is strongly driven by line count and quantity; unit price shows a weaker association, so value growth comes mainly from basket size rather than price.
captions.cancellation_trends.png: Monthly cancellation invoice counts. Cancellations occur throughout the year and peak in the high-volume autumn months, tracking overall activity rather than a single incident.
captions.weekday_sales.png: Revenue by day of week. Weekday trading dominates; the weekend share is materially lower, which has direct implications for staffing and promotional scheduling.
captions.hourly_patterns.png: Order volume by hour of day. Activity is concentrated in business hours with a clear midday peak, consistent with B2B-style buying behaviour.
captions.pareto_chart.png: Pareto curve of customer revenue concentration. The curve rises steeply at the top, showing that a minority of customers generates the majority of revenue; the 80% threshold is reached at 1,130 customers.
captions.top_customers.png: Top 10 customers by net revenue. The leading account alone contributes a material share of total revenue, creating concentration risk that management should monitor.
captions.rfm_scatter.png: RFM map of a 3,000-customer random sample. Recent, high-value customers (Champions) sit in the top-left; long-inactive high-value accounts (Can't Lose / At Risk) appear in the top-right and represent the clearest win-back opportunity.

opportunities.Evidence: Can't Lose + At Risk segments contain 658 customers worth £818,897
opportunities.Business problem: Previously valuable customers have stopped purchasing, leaving revenue exposed.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Targeted win-back campaign with personalised offers and a service-level check-in.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Recover a share of lapsed high-value revenue; protect the revenue base.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Win-back conversion rate; recovered revenue per campaign.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Historical response behaviour is unknown; campaign lift must be measured with a control group.

opportunities.Opportunity: Grow basket size rather than unit price
opportunities.Evidence: Spearman rho between invoice value and line count = 0.55, versus 0.09 for average price
opportunities.Business problem: Revenue is driven mainly by number of lines, not by higher prices.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Cross-sell bundles and 'complete the set' recommendations at checkout.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Higher items per order without discounting, protecting margin.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Average lines per invoice; attach rate; AOV.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Cross-sell may cannibalise existing lines; test on a holdout group.

opportunities.Opportunity: Concentrate retention effort on the revenue core
opportunities.Evidence: Top 26.1% of customers (1,130 accounts) generate 80% of revenue; top 1% generate 31.8%
opportunities.Business problem: Revenue is highly concentrated, so losing a few accounts is material.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Named-account management and service guarantees for the top revenue accounts.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Reduced churn risk on the highest-value relationships.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Revenue retention of top-decile accounts; churn of top 100 accounts.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Over-serving small accounts could distort cost-to-serve; concentration remains a structural risk.

opportunities.Opportunity: Replicate the UK playbook in selected EU markets
opportunities.Evidence: UK contributes 84.6% of revenue; Germany is the largest non-UK market at £228,678
opportunities.Business problem: Growth depends almost entirely on one market.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Localise catalogue, pricing and delivery messaging for the top 3 EU markets.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Diversified revenue base and reduced single-market exposure.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Non-UK revenue share; non-UK repeat rate; delivery cost per order.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Cross-border logistics and pricing differences may erode margin; results are not transferable without testing.

opportunities.Evidence: 3,836 cancellation invoices (16.12% of invoices) with £893,980 gross value
opportunities.Business problem: Returns and cancellations remove revenue after the sale is booked.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Pre-purchase quality checks, clearer sizing guidance and a cancellation-reason code.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Lower cancellation rate and better root-cause visibility.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Cancellation rate by product and reason code; net revenue per SKU.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Some cancellations are genuine commercial returns; reducing them too aggressively harms customer trust.

opportunities.Opportunity: Extend the seasonal peak with an early-autumn campaign
opportunities.Evidence: Peak month is Nov 2011 at £1,503,867; order volume peaks in the same period
opportunities.Business problem: Revenue is concentrated in a short seasonal window, creating capacity and cash-flow swings.
opportunities.Proposed solution: Shift a defined share of promotional spend to September–October and pre-build stock.
opportunities.Expected benefit: Smoother revenue, better inventory utilisation, lower peak-season stress.
opportunities.KPI to monitor: Off-season revenue growth; stock cover; peak-season service level.
opportunities.Risk / limitation: Demand may simply be pulled forward rather than created; measure incremental, not shifted, revenue.

findings: F1
Revenue is highly concentrated in time and in customers.
Peak month Nov 2011 generated £1,503,867; the top 1% of customers generate 31.8% of revenue.
Demand is seasonal and the customer base is top-heavy.
Build seasonal capacity plans and protect top accounts.
F2
The 80/20 rule holds for customers but only approximately.
1,130 customers (26.1%) produce 80% of revenue; the top 20% produce 74.7%.
Concentration is real but not exactly 80/20; the curve is steeper at the very top.
Prioritise retention of the top 20% and monitor the top 1% for churn.
F3
Revenue is driven by basket size, not price.
Spearman rho (invoice value vs lines) = 0.55; (invoice value vs average price) = 0.09.
Customers spend more by adding lines rather than accepting higher prices.
Use cross-sell and bundling instead of price increases.
F4
The UK dominates the revenue base.
UK revenue = £9,001,744 (84.6% of total); the largest non-UK market is Germany.
Geographic concentration is a material business risk.
Diversify into selected EU markets with localised offers.
F5
Repeat purchase is the norm among identified customers, but a large anonymous base exists.
2,845 of 4,338 identified customers (65.6%) ordered more than once; 135,080 lines have no CustomerID.
Identified customers are loyal, but 25% of activity cannot be attributed.
Incentivise account creation / loyalty sign-up to close the attribution gap.
F6
Cancellations are a persistent, material leakage.
3,836 cancellation invoices (16.12% of invoices) with £893,980 gross value.
Returns reduce realised revenue and complicate demand forecasting.
Introduce cancellation reason codes and product-level quality checks.
F7
Extreme values are genuine commercial events, not errors.
Largest valid line: 80,995 units of PAPER CRAFT , LITTLE BIRDIE (£168,470).
Wholesale-style purchases exist and materially affect totals.
Retain outliers in headline totals; report medians alongside means.
F8
Customer value is highly unequal.
Top customer 14646 contributes £280,206 (2.6% of revenue); top 10 contribute 14.4%.
A small number of accounts carry a large share of revenue.
Create named-account plans and monitor concentration risk.
F9
Non-UK customers place materially higher-value orders, but the effect size is small.
UK mean AOV £500 vs non-UK £845; medians £300 vs £424; Welch p = 1.80e-16, Cohen's d = -0.19.
The difference is statistically significant but small in magnitude, so it should not drive a wholesale pricing change.
Test market-specific shipping thresholds and promotions rather than assuming a uniform international price premium.
Repeat customers buy more consistently, but not at a higher average order value.
Mean AOV £421 (repeat) vs £411 (one-time), Welch p = 0.87, d = 0.01; medians £303 vs £256, Mann–Whitney p = 8.56e-12.
The means are indistinguishable, but the whole distribution is shifted upward for repeat buyers — loyalty improves basket consistency rather than average value.
Do not assume loyalty automatically raises AOV; measure basket-building interventions separately from retention.
Trading is concentrated on weekdays and business hours.
Peak day Thursday (revenue £2,199,293); peak hour 12:00 with 3,220 invoices.
Demand follows a B2B-style weekly rhythm.
Align staffing, dispatch and campaign sends to the observed rhythm.
Product revenue sits in a long tail, not in a handful of hero products.
The top 10 products account for only 9.4% of product revenue; 825 of 3,912 products (21.1%) are needed to reach 80%.
Unlike the customer base, the catalogue is not dominated by a few items; 3,912 products share the revenue.
Manage the tail actively (rationalisation, availability) instead of assuming a few hero SKUs carry the business.
